items.stem: State the condition on the two reaction rates that defines equilibrium in a reversible reaction.
items.modelAnswer: Equilibrium is reached when the rates of the forward and reverse reactions become equal.

items.stem: State the system condition a reversible reaction needs before equilibrium can be reached.
items.modelAnswer: A closed system is required, so no species can leave the vessel and nothing can enter.

items.stem: Explain why a reversible reaction reaches equilibrium instead of running to completion.
items.modelAnswer: Because a reversible reaction runs in both the forward and reverse directions: as products build up the reverse reaction runs faster, until the two rates become equal at equilibrium.

items.stem: A student claims that a reaction mixture at equilibrium must contain equal amounts of reactants and products. Use what stays constant at equilibrium to answer the claim.
items.modelAnswer: The claim is wrong: at equilibrium it is the concentrations of reactants and products that stay constant while nothing else changes, which is not the same as saying the amounts are equal.

items.stem: State the industrial process used in the note as the example of a reaction reaching equilibrium.
items.modelAnswer: The Haber process, run in a sealed container.

items.stem: State the vessel condition under which the Haber process reaches equilibrium.
items.modelAnswer: It runs in a sealed container, forming a closed system.

items.stem: Explain why the backward reaction speeds up as the Haber process proceeds.
items.modelAnswer: Because the ammonia concentration rises as the reaction proceeds, and the backward reaction decomposes ammonia back into nitrogen and hydrogen, so more ammonia means a faster backward reaction.

items.stem: A sealed Haber vessel has run for several hours: the amounts of nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia have stopped changing. State which reaction is faster at that moment, the forward or the backward.
items.modelAnswer: Neither — the two rates have become equal, because equilibrium has been reached.

items.stem: State the term for a large molecule of high relative molecular mass built from many joined monomers.
items.modelAnswer: A polymer.

items.stem: State the name of the reaction that joins monomers together.
items.modelAnswer: Addition polymerisation.

items.stem: Explain what happens to each monomer when it joins the growing polymer chain.
items.modelAnswer: Each monomer becomes a repeat unit, connected to its neighbours by covalent bonds.

items.stem: A factory manufactures a new material by joining thousands of small molecules into one giant chain. State whether the new material is a natural or a synthetic polymer.
items.modelAnswer: A synthetic polymer — manufactured polymers like plastics and nylon are synthetic, while nature makes the natural or biological polymers.

items.stem: State the name of the polymer formed when ethene undergoes addition polymerisation.
items.modelAnswer: Polyethene.

items.stem: State the rule for building an addition polymer's name from its monomer's name.
items.modelAnswer: Take the monomer's name in brackets and add poly- in front of it.

items.stem: Explain why the finished polymer chain contains only single bonds even though each monomer carries a C=C double bond.
items.modelAnswer: Because one of the two bonds in each C=C double bond breaks, and that bond forms the link to the adjacent monomer, leaving the chain with single bonds only.

items.stem: Chloroethene is the monomer used to make PVC. State the systematic name of the polymer it forms, following the note's naming rule.
items.modelAnswer: Polychloroethene — the rule puts poly- in front of the monomer's name, chloroethene, in brackets.

items.stem: State what happens to the other groups around the former double bond when a monomer is drawn as a repeat unit.
items.modelAnswer: They keep the same order they had around the double bond in the monomer.

items.stem: State where the bonds at each end of a repeat unit must extend.
items.modelAnswer: Outside the brackets — one bond at each end, extending beyond them.

items.stem: Explain why changing the single bond back to a double bond recovers the monomer from a repeat unit.
items.modelAnswer: Because drawing the repeat unit changed the monomer's double bond to a single bond and added the two end bonds; reversing those steps, and removing the end bonds and the n, gives back the original monomer.

items.stem: A student draws a repeat unit with both end bonds inside the brackets and no subscript n. State the two corrections needed to make the drawing correct.
items.modelAnswer: Move the end bonds so they extend outside the brackets, and add the subscript n on the bottom right.

items.stem: A cup of sugar water is made by stirring sugar into hot tea. State which substance is the solvent.
items.modelAnswer: The tea (the water in it) is the solvent — the liquid doing the dissolving.

items.stem: State the term for the mixture formed once a solute has dissolved in a solvent.
items.modelAnswer: A solution.

items.stem: Explain why no more salt can dissolve in a solution that is already saturated.
items.modelAnswer: Because a saturated solution already holds the maximum amount of dissolved solute the solvent can take, so no more solute can be dissolved.

items.stem: A student keeps stirring sugar into tea until some sugar sits at the bottom and will not dissolve, however long they stir. State the term describing the tea at that moment.
items.modelAnswer: The tea is a saturated solution — it holds the maximum amount of dissolved solute the solvent can take.

items.stem: State the relationship between the total mass of the reactants and the total mass of the products in any chemical reaction.
items.modelAnswer: The total mass of the reactants always equals the total mass of the products.

items.stem: State what happens to the atoms of the reactants during a chemical reaction.
items.modelAnswer: New substances form, but the same atoms are present before and after — every atom in the reactants must appear in the products.

items.stem: Explain why no atoms disappear during a chemical reaction.
items.modelAnswer: Because atoms cannot be created or destroyed — they are only rearranged into the new substances, so every reactant atom survives into the products.

items.stem: 12.0 g of magnesium burns completely in 8.0 g of oxygen inside a sealed flask. State the mass of magnesium oxide formed.
items.modelAnswer: 20.0 g — the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products (conservation of mass).

items.stem: State which side of a word equation the products are written on.
items.modelAnswer: The right-hand side — reactants sit on the left of the arrow and products on the right.

items.stem: State the term for the chemical ingredients of a reaction, mixed together before it starts.
items.modelAnswer: The reactants.

items.stem: Explain why the reactants are named before the products when a word equation is written.
items.modelAnswer: Because the reactants are the ingredients mixed together before the reaction starts, and the arrow then signals their conversion into the products — the order follows the course of the reaction.

items.stem: Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide. State the word equation for the reaction.
items.modelAnswer: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide.

items.stem: State the four state symbols used in balanced chemical equations.
items.modelAnswer: Solid (s), liquid (l), gas (g) and aqueous (aq).

items.stem: State how an unchanged group such as the nitrate group is counted when balancing an equation.
items.modelAnswer: Count it as one entity, instead of balancing its individual atoms separately.

items.stem: Explain why the nitrate group can be balanced as one entity rather than atom by atom.
items.modelAnswer: Because the group stays unchanged through the reaction — it passes from the reactant to the product as one unit, so counting it as one entity keeps the balance correct.

items.stem: Copper(II) sulfate solution reacts with sodium hydroxide solution, and both solutes are dissolved in water. State the state symbol each of the two reactants carries in the balanced equation.
items.modelAnswer: Aqueous, (aq) — both reactants are dissolved in water.
